title: Resources and Development — Chapter Summary
intro: A RESOURCE is anything in the environment that we can use, given the right technology, economics and culture. Resources are not 'gifts of nature' — they are the result of an interaction between nature, technology and institutions. This chapter classifies resources, traces the threats to them, lays out the steps of resource planning, and goes deep into India's most basic resources: LAND and SOIL — including their degradation and conservation.

sections.heading: What is a Resource?
bullets: A resource is anything in the environment that satisfies human needs.
Three conditions: technologically accessible, economically feasible, culturally acceptable.
Resources are produced by interaction between nature, technology and institutions.
They are unevenly distributed in nature.

sections.heading: Classification of Resources
bullets: ORIGIN: biotic (living) vs abiotic (non-living).
EXHAUSTIBILITY: renewable (solar, wind, forests) vs non-renewable (coal, petroleum).
OWNERSHIP: individual / community / national / international.
STATUS: potential / developed / STOCK (tech missing) / RESERVES (tech ready, postponed).

sections.heading: Development of Resources and the Rio Earth Summit
bullets: Indiscriminate use creates inequality and ecological crisis.
SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT — meeting present needs without harming future generations.
Earth Summit at Rio (1992) — 100+ heads of state.
Agenda 21 — global plan for sustainable development; every local body to draw its own.
Gandhi: 'There is enough for everybody's need and not for anybody's greed.'

sections.heading: Resource Planning in India
bullets: Step 1: identification and inventory of resources — survey + mapping + estimation.
Step 2: planning structure with technology, skill and institutions.
Step 3: matching the plan with national development plans.
Different states have different mixes — Jharkhand minerals; Rajasthan solar/wind; Arunachal water; Ladakh tourism.

sections.heading: Land Resources and Degradation
bullets: India's geographical area ≈ 3.28 million sq km.
43% plains, 30% mountains, 27% plateaus.
Land use categories — forests, NA-cultivation, fallow, NSA, GCA.
About 130 million ha of land is degraded.
Causes: deforestation due to mining (Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh); over-grazing (Gujarat, Rajasthan, MP); over-irrigation → salinity (Punjab, Haryana, W-UP).
Conservation: afforestation, shelter belts, sand-dune stabilisation, mining control.

sections.heading: Soils of India
bullets: Soil is the most important RENEWABLE natural resource — but takes millions of years to form.
ALLUVIAL — northern plains and deltas; Bangar (old) and Khadar (new); fertile.
BLACK / REGUR — Deccan basalt; clayey; great moisture-holding; ideal for COTTON.
RED & YELLOW — Deccan crystalline rocks; iron-rich.
LATERITE — high rain + heat; leached; needs manure; suitable for tea, coffee, cashew.
ARID — sandy, saline, low humus; western Rajasthan.
FOREST — hilly / mountainous areas with rain forests.

sections.heading: Soil Erosion and Conservation
bullets: Erosion = denudation of the soil cover.
Gully erosion — deep channels (Chambal ravines / bad lands).
Sheet erosion — topsoil washed away over a slope.
Wind erosion — loose soil blown off flat / sloping land.
Conservation: contour ploughing, terrace cultivation, strip cropping, shelter belts.

key_takeaways: A resource is anything we can use, given the right technology, economics and culture.
Resources are classified by origin, exhaustibility, ownership and status.
Indiscriminate use creates inequality and ecological crisis; sustainable development is the response.
The 1992 Earth Summit and Agenda 21 set the global framework.
Resource planning has three steps: survey, planning structure, integration.
India's land is 43% plains, 30% mountains, 27% plateaus; ~130 million ha is degraded.
Major Indian soils: alluvial, black/regur, red-yellow, laterite, arid, forest.
Soil erosion is countered by contour ploughing, terraces, strip cropping and shelter belts.

glossary.definition: Anything in the environment that can be used to satisfy human needs, given technology, economics and culture allow.
Resources derived from the living world — humans, plants, animals, fish.
Resources from non-living things — rocks, minerals, water, sunlight.
A resource that can be renewed by natural processes within a useful time.
A resource formed over millions of years and exhausted far faster than it can renew.
Materials in the environment that could meet human needs but for which the right technology is not yet available.
A subset of stock that can be put into use with present technology, but whose use has been postponed.
Development that meets present needs without compromising the needs of future generations.
The 1992 Rio declaration — a global plan of action for sustainable development.
Old (Bangar) and new (Khadar) alluvial soils; Khadar is more fertile.
Black cotton soil of the Deccan trap, formed on basalt lava flows.
Soil formed in regions of high temperature and rainfall by leaching that removes lime and silica.
Loss of productivity of land due to deforestation, over-grazing, mining or over-irrigation.
Removal of a thin layer of topsoil by water flowing as a sheet over a slope.
Rows of trees planted to slow wind and reduce wind-erosion of soil.
